hints: Separate as e^(−2y)dy = kx/(x²+1) dx and integrate both sides.
Use y=0 at x=0 to find the constant, then y=−1/2 at x=1 to determine k exactly.
Substitute x=√3 into the resulting relation, isolate e^(−2y), and take logarithms for the exact y-value.
walkthrough:
Use the initial condition $y = 0$ when $x = 0$ to find the constant $C$:
$$-\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{e}^0 = \dfrac{k}{2}\ln(0 + 1) + C \implies -\dfrac{1}{2}(1) = \dfrac{k}{2}(0) + C \implies C = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$-\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{e}^{-2y} = \dfrac{k}{2}\ln(x^2 + 1) - \dfrac{1}{2}$$

Use the condition $y = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $x = 1$ to find $k$:
$$\mathrm{e}^{-2(-1/2)} = 1 - k\ln(1^2 + 1)$$
$$\mathrm{e}^1 = 1 - k\ln(2)$$
$$k\ln(2) = 1 - \mathrm{e} \implies k = \dfrac{1 - \mathrm{e}}{\ln(2)}$$

Write down the particular solution relating $x$ and $y$:
$$\mathrm{e}^{-2y} = 1 - \left(\dfrac{1 - \mathrm{e}}{\ln(2)}\right)\ln(x^2 + 1)$$

Solve for $y$ by taking the natural logarithm:
$$-2y = \ln(2\mathrm{e} - 1) \implies y = -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2\mathrm{e} - 1)$$
